item.title: From Classical Trapping to Curvature-Induced Bolus Formation in Peristaltic Wave-Driven Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.24219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bolus formation is one of the most distinctive features of peristaltic transport, yet the mechanisms governing its development remain incompletely understood. In this work, axisymmetric peristaltic-wave-driven flows under zero-pressure-gradient conditions are investigated using a high-fidelity lattice Boltzmann framework over a broad range of wave amplitudes, wavelengths, and Reynolds numbers spanning the Stokes limit to Re=100. In the Stokes limit, bolus formation is governed by the classical trapping mechanism and exhibits a remarkable wavelength-normalized similarity, with both bolus morphology and transport characteristics approaching common asymptotic behaviors as the wavelength increases. As fluid inertia becomes significant, this similarity progressively breaks down and wavelength-dependent trapping behavior emerges. In the short-wavelength regime, the pronounced geometric bending of the wave reorganizes the local flow structure and produces a distinct off-axis bolus associated with a curvature-induced trapping mechanism. The influence of this mechanism expands toward longer wavelengths with increasing Reynolds number and occupies an increasingly large portion of the parameter space considered in the present study. The results reveal that bolus formation cannot be described by a single universal mechanism. Instead, the observed trapping behavior arises from the competition between classical trapping and curvature-induced trapping, whose relative importance is controlled by wavelength, wave amplitude, and Reynolds number. These findings establish a unified physical framework for understanding bolus formation and transport in peristaltic-wave-driven flows.
item.dc:creator: Lucija Josipovic, Melissa Reyes Munoz, Fernando Mendez Estrada, Hui Wan, Fangjun Shu, Yanxing Wang

item.title: A consistent coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid solver for two-phase flow in OpenFOAM
item.description: arXiv:2610.24225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid methods combine the mass conservation of a transported volume fraction with the smooth interface description of a signed-distance function. In the simple coupled variant, the level set is rebuilt from the volume fraction during every time step rather than transported, and it supplies the interface curvature and the fluid properties. This paper presents an implementation of the simple coupled method in OpenFOAM and sets out four conditions that such an implementation must satisfy to stay consistent. The density in the time derivative and in the convective mass flux of the momentum equation must be the same field, the curvature in the surface tension force must come from the level set, the blended kinematic viscosity must reproduce the blended dynamic viscosity, and the smoothed fields must be evaluated on boundary and processor patches as well as in the cells. The solver is tested on the second two-dimensional rising-bubble case of Hysing et al. on two meshes. Up to t= 1.75 s, while the three reference codes of that benchmark agree, the rise velocity differs from the reference by at most 0.0064 and 0.0073 m/s on the two meshes, and its first maximum is 1.3% and 2.0% below the reference. These differences grow slightly with refinement. The same happens when the curvature and the properties are taken from the volume fraction, which reproduces the standard OpenFOAM solver, so their cause lies outside the coupling. Over the same interval the level-set coupling stays closer to the reference than this volume-fraction coupling, with a largest velocity difference of 0.0073 against 0.0094 m/s on the finer mesh. The bubble volume is conserved to the printed precision, and a run on four processors matches the serial run. The solver is released under the GNU General Public License.
item.dc:creator: Amirhossein Taran

item.title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.24689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way that only one of the CRW is affected and controlled by a single parameter representing the asymmetry, via modifying the bottom background potential vorticity gradient. We derive conditions where the instantaneous growths have key CRW properties that are independent of the asymmetry parameter for a reasonably general family of norms, and that the instability characteristic in the total energy norm is entirely independent of the asymmetry parameter. For finite time transient growth, the optimal initial condition is in some sense counter to that of the exponential growing normal mode: where the bottom slope is such that it is strengthening the bottom CRW, the normal mode has a larger bottom CRW, but the finite time optimal initial condition wants the bottom CRW to be weak instead, and vice-versa. While the results presented here are for the sloped Eady problem, the same results were also found for an analogous Phillips problem, and we speculate the instability characteristics may have origins in the underlying symmetries that are common to those two problems.
item.dc:creator: J. Yin, N. Harnik, E. Heifetz, J. Mak

item.title: Yielding-dependent Taylor dispersion in electrokinetic-magnetohydrodynamic Casson microflows
item.description: arXiv:2610.25433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal dispersion in a yielding fluid depends on the velocity distribution and on how the flow is maintained. We study a neutral tracer in pressure-assisted electrokinetic and magnetohydrodynamic flow of a Casson fluid through a slit microchannel. The nonlinear stress and velocity equations determine the yielded layers, the unyielded core and the axial flow. Mei's multiple-scale homogenization of the advection-diffusion equation then separates transverse relaxation, mean drift and longitudinal spreading, yielding the Taylor-Aris auxiliary problem and effective diffusivity. An exact pressure-driven solution gives cubic decay of the mean velocity and eighth-power decay of the dispersion enhancement near flow arrest. Under fixed pressure and electrical forcing, increasing the yield parameter from $Y=0$ to $0.7$ moves the optimum Hartmann number from $Ha_p=0.696$ to $2.634$, while the corresponding normalized diffusivity decreases from $D_T^{\mathrm C}=1.454$ to $1.015$. At fixed mean throughput and $Ha_p=1$, the trend reverses: $D_T^{\mathrm C}$ increases from $1.000433$ to $1.002311$. The homogenized energy identity traces this difference to the velocity departure from the sectional mean, including that within the unyielded core. Analytical limiting solutions, direct concentration calculations, numerical convergence studies and a coupled Casson shear test support the reduced-flow predictions. An electrolyte-based dimensional assessment identifies the magnetic optima as theoretical forcing states for representative aqueous microchannels. These results are relevant to predicting longitudinal tracer spreading in microchannels carrying fluids with a yield stress, whether pressure or throughput is controlled.
item.dc:creator: Nanda Poddar, Debabrata Das, Suman Chakraborty

item.title: Probing Flow-Induced Chain Scission in Shear-Banding Wormlike Micelles
item.description: arXiv:2610.25442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the microstructural dynamics of wormlike micellar (WLM) solutions based on CPyCl/NaSal/D\(_2\)O under shear flow using spatially resolved rheo-diffusion NMR, velocity-compensated diffusion measurements, and rheo-optical imaging in a Taylor--Couette geometry. Two viscoelastic systems were examined: a non-shear-banding WLM with a molar salt-surfactant concentration ratio of \(R=0.4\) and a shear-banding WLM with \(R=0.53\). Rheo-optical and velocity measurements confirm homogeneous flow for the non-shear-banding system and the coexistence of low- and high-shear bands within the stress-plateau regime for the shear-banding system. Despite the pronounced heterogeneity in velocity and shear rate associated with shear banding, the local surfactant self-diffusivity remains spatially uniform across the gap and throughout the stress-plateau regime. Furthermore, analysis of the mean-squared-displacement scaling reveals no measurable difference between the high- and low-shear bands. These results demonstrate that the micellar microstructure remains largely unchanged despite the formation of shear bands and provide direct experimental evidence that flow-induced micellar chain scission is not a dominant mechanism governing shear banding in this WLM system.
item.dc:creator: Alfredo Scigliani, Samuel C. Grant, Hadi Mohammadigoushki

item.title: Fractal forcing of turbulence by settling particles
item.description: arXiv:2610.26050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The settling of particles in a fluid medium can trigger complex collective dynamics, dramatically affecting the distribution of energy across flow scales. In this work we present the first fully-resolved observations of the turbulence induced by large particle structures, also known as cluster-induced-turbulence (CIT), obtained through particle-resolved direct numerical simulations at high volume fractions and density ratios in large domains. We find that particles arrange in macroscopic fractal structures, exciting turbulent fluctuations at scales much larger than the individual constituents. By virtue of their fractal nature, these clusters force the continuous-phase in a multiscale, self-similar way. We further show that these cluster-driven, vertically decorrelated fluctuations at large scales coexist with, but are fundamentally distinct from, the established particle-driven high-wavenumber scaling. Beyond unveiling a different form of clustering in particle-settling, these results highlight a naturally arising, self-assembling path to fractal-generated turbulence.
item.dc:creator: Simone Tandurella, Alessandro Chiarini, Marco Edoardo Rosti

item.title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.26164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape (zeros of $\mathbf v(\mathbf x,t)$) are non-generic yet common; we derive their motion. Differentiating $\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ gives $\mathbf L\mathbf U=-\mathbf a$ ($\mathbf U$ curve velocity, $\mathbf a=\mathbf v_t$, $\mathbf L=\nabla\mathbf v$ kills tangent, acts on normal plane via $2\times2$ block $\mathbf K$); dynamics enters only via $\mathbf a$. Normal velocity: $-\mathbf K^{-1}$ times normal $\mathbf a$; tangential solvability: scalar condition $\Sigma=0$ per point ($\Sigma$: part of $\mathbf a$ outside range $\mathbf L$). Potential flow: $\mathbf K$ is strain rate, normal velocity pressure gradient over principal strain rate $\epsilon$, persistence needs uniform pressure on it. Stokes flow: tangential vorticity enters $\mathbf K$ (centre lines), $\Sigma$ involves normal vorticity. Navier-Stokes: $\Sigma$ set by instantaneous flow via nonlocal pressure, viscosity. If $\Sigma\ne0$, line becomes, to first order in $t$, isolated points at zeros of $\Sigma$ (critical points of $\varphi_t$ if potential; maybe none in Stokes flow: loops vanish). Symmetry (line an orbit of rigid-motion group, no velocity along it) suffices for persistence, not necessary: flows steady in rigidly moving frame have $\Sigma\equiv0$. Incompressibility enters via $\mathrm{tr}\mathbf K=0$; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow, line dilatation is $\varphi_{tt}/c^2$, so lines can be nodes, persistence needs uniform enthalpy, singular $\mathbf K$ arises at ordinary points, acoustic standing waves give exact examples (node line breaking into alternating sinks, saddles); also degenerate $\mathbf K$ (pairs born at distance $O(\sqrt t)$), curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow, exact Navier-Stokes example: saddle, centre lines split into four points per period.
item.dc:creator: Prabakaran Rajamanickam

item.title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.26567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.
item.dc:creator: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi

item.title: Bridging the Lattice Boltzmann Method and Moment Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.26631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) and identify the general moment closure shared by kinetic methods based on the discrete-velocity Boltzmann equation. This closure provides a route to correct lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate reconstruction of the higher-order moments, thereby substantially broadening the scope of existing closure strategies that seek increasingly accurate representations of these moments. These advances establish a unified moment framework bridging LBM and moment methods. The framework enables efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes, overcoming the prohibitive complexity of existing moment methods at high Knudsen numbers. It further provides a common basis for integrating and extending key features of diverse kinetic methods.
item.dc:creator: Jinhua Lu, Song Zhao, Pierre Sagaut, Nikolaus A. Adams

item.title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.26694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread and exploits the structure of flow-solver kernels: pure accumulations need no tape, the remaining intermediate values are recomputed rather than stored, and adjoint updates are atomic only where several threads reach the same memory. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models: a viscous Burgers residual, a two-dimensional advection-diffusion residual, a quasi-one-dimensional Euler residual and a Biot-Savart summation over point vortices. All generated derivatives agree with finite differences and pass adjoint dot-product tests to round-off, while the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. Compared with the compiler-based tool Clad under the same compiler, CuAD gives identical results at identical cost on the stencil kernels and is 16 to 470 times faster on the summation kernel because it stores no tape. A steady Burgers study shows that in single precision the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent once the condition number grows to $2.5\times10^{5}$, whereas the CuAD Jacobian keeps the error below $5\times10^{-5}$. Four applications complete the evaluation: adjoint fields of the Burgers shock, the sensitivity of a scalar sensor in a cellular vortex, the inverse design of a transonic nozzle whose area is recovered to $2\times10^{-8}$, and an unsteady adjoint of the roll-up of a vortex sheet over 400 time steps.
item.dc:creator: Seunghyun Joo

item.title: Magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor instability driven by a rotating magnetic field: Cylindrical liner configuration
item.description: arXiv:1711.08891v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose using a directional time-varying (rotating) driving magnetic field to suppress magneto-Rayleigh-Taylor (MRT) instability in dynamic Z-pinches. A rotational drive magnetic field is equivalent to two magnetic-field components, {\Theta} and Z, that alternate in time, referred to as an alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration. We consider the finitely thick cylindrical liner configuration in this paper. We numerically integrate the perturbation equation to stagnation time based on the optimal background unperturbed trajectories. We assess the cumulative growth of the dominant mode selected by some mechanism at the beginning of an implosion. The maximum e-folding number at stagnation of the dominant mode of an optimized alternate Theta-Z-pinch is significantly lower than that of the standard Theta- or Z-pinch. The directional rotation of the magnetic field contributes to suppress the instabilities, independent of the finite thickness. The finite thickness effect plays a role only when the orientation of the magnetic field varies in time whereas it does not appear in the standard Theta- or Z-pinch. The rotating frequency of the magnetic field and the thickness of liner are both having a monotonic effect on suppression. Their synergistic effect can enhance the suppression on MRT instability. Because the MRT instability can be well suppressed in this way, the alternate Theta-Z-pinch configuration has potential applications in liner inertial fusion. This work is supported by the NSFC (Grant Nos. 11405167, 51407171, 11571293, 11605188, and 11605189) and the Foundation of the China Academy of Engineering Physics (No. 2015B0201023).
item.dc:creator: Shu-Chao Duan, Long Yang, Bo Xiao, Ming-Xian Kan, Gang-Hua Wang, Wei-Ping Xie

item.title: Residual Carleman lift for nonlinear lattice Boltzmann simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.24041v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-order Carleman embeddings replace nonlinear dynamics by a larger linear system, but truncation errors can accumulate even when the underlying nonlinear model is accurately approximated by a quadratic equation. We construct a residual Carleman lift (RC2) of lattice Boltzmann dynamics in which an independently evolved spectral background supplies the coefficients and forcing of a second-order residual lift. In a double-shear-layer test, conventional fixed-rest Carleman reaches $87.3\%$ final error, whereas prepared RC2 achieves $0.136\%$ through vortex roll-up, without restarting the lift or using fine-reference feedback. The results demonstrate control of the finite-time accuracy of a fixed-order linear embedding through nonlinear preparation.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Karlin

item.title: Probing wetting and solidification dynamics of neon thin films with a high-$T_c$ superconducting circuit
item.description: arXiv:2610.24167v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Integrating condensed noble gases with superconducting circuits offers new opportunities for operating hybrid quantum devices. In particular, electrons on solid neon have recently emerged as exceptionally coherent charge qubits, however the growth of the underlying neon films on patterned devices remains poorly controlled. We monitor neon films near the triple point using a multimode resonator fabricated from high-$T_c$ YBCO, which remains superconducting at temperatures where the liquid phase exists and whose geometry sets a thickness-sensing window near 1 $\mu$m. In the liquid state we observe rich film dynamics: uniform wetting that saturates near 20 nm, drainage of thicker films, and spontaneous thickness oscillations, reflecting the extreme sensitivity of thick films in this regime. A galvanic connection to our sensing volume enables in-situ electrostatic tuning of the liquid film thickness. Statistics of freezing the neon across various liquid levels reveal variations of the solid film thickness by approximately an order of magnitude. We also observe a two-fold increase in the quality factor of the resonators at the level of $10^3$ with added neon and rule out dielectric loss as the limiting factor. Our results demonstrate that hermetic packaging facilitates the investigation of both rich non-equilibrium fluid dynamics and the impact of condensed noble gas films on microwave loss in superconducting circuits, but may not be the best modality for growing solid neon films with precisely controlled thickness.
item.dc:creator: Brennan Dizdar, Yueheng Shi, David I. Schuster, Christopher S. Lang

item.title: Colour-Field Based Particle Categorization for Residual Stress Detection and Reduction in Solid SPH Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.24210v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics has been extensively used in solid mechanics simulations and the inherent colour-field generation approach is a promising tracker for the residual stress. In this paper, we propose a way to use the colour-field approach for eliminating the residual stress and prevent the undesirable premature failure of solid objects.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: In Proceedings of the 18th International Joint Conference on Computer Vision, Imaging and Computer Graphics Theory and Applications (VISIGRAPP 2023) - Volume 1: GRAPP, pages 237-241
item.dc:creator: Gizem Kayar

item.title: Calibrated shape-only recovery of membrane viscosities
item.description: arXiv:2610.24410v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearby relaxation rates make two membrane viscosities difficult to distinguish from a shape transient. We show how calibrated preparation removes this loss of local sensitivity in a linear Kelvin-Voigt sphere with finite area elasticity and intrinsic membrane dissipation. Two independent releases, with a known signed amplitude ratio and calibrated relative gain and timing, yield normal-displacement records whose fixed linear combination separates the shear and dilatational rates. Their common amplitude remains unknown. For fixed sampling, positive-definite weights, bounded positive rates and nonzero excitation, the amplitude-projected sensitivity has a positive lower bound even at rate coincidence. Without relative calibration, the paired sensitivity decreases linearly with the rate gap; the single tangential-release record decreases quadratically. The calibrated bound is compatible with fixed finite initial energy. A positive local bound also persists with independent ratio calibration of fixed positive precision under a Gaussian error model. Supplied elastic coefficients convert the recovered rates into the two surface viscosities. An unbounded spherical Stokes extension quantifies how bulk dissipation changes the modal patterns and provides a sufficient full-Jacobian criterion for retaining local material sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Julian Olszewski, Zijian Liu, Jie Xu

item.title: Micrometer-thin liquid sheets from single-jet impact on a sharp edge for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.24504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a simple and robust method for generating freely suspended liquid sheets by directing a single laminar liquid jet onto the sharp edge of an inclined plate. By optimizing liquid composition, impact geometry, and flow conditions, we identify a 60:40 ethylene-glycol-deionized-water volumetric mixture for stable sheet formation. The resulting sheets span 8 mm in height and 3 mm in width, with thicknesses from 1.1 to 4.8 micrometers measured by spatial and spectral interferometry. Operated in vacuum as continuously renewed plasma mirrors, these targets demonstrate stable performance from 0.5 to 10 kHz using 175-fs Yb:KGW laser pulses, reaching a maximum S-polarized reflectivity of 66.5% at an intensity of 4 x 10^14 W/cm^2. At higher intensities using 25-fs Ti:sapphire pulses at 1 kHz, maximum S-polarized reflectivity reaches 77% at 2 x 10^16 W/cm^2. The reflected beam exhibits high temporal stability, with angular pointing fluctuations of 18.19 +/- 0.53 microradians. Our results demonstrate a tunable, continuously renewed liquid-sheet target for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments.
item.dc:creator: Mukesh Kumar, S. Sree Harsha, Prashant Kumar Singh

item.title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2610.24876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.
item.dc:creator: Yinghe Qi, Qutadah Rababah, Wei Guo

item.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
item.description: arXiv:2610.24934v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.
item.dc:creator: Ryan D. Maladen, Yang Ding, Chen Li, Daniel I. Goldman

item.title: Dependence of the acoustic propulsion of nano- and microcones on their orientation and aspect ratio
item.description: arXiv:2610.25383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent research revealed the orientation-dependent propulsion of a cone-shaped colloidal particle that is exposed to a planar traveling ultrasound wave. Here, we extend the previous research by considering nano- and microcones with different aspect ratios and studying how the propulsion of a particle depends on its orientation and aspect ratio. We also study how the orientation-averaged propulsion of a cone-shaped particle, which corresponds to an isotropic ultrasound field, depends on its aspect ratio and identify an aspect ratio of 1/2 where the orientation-averaged propulsion is particularly strong. To make our simulation results easier reusable for follow-up research, we provide a corresponding simple analytic representation.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Vo\ss{}, Raphael Wittkowski

item.title: Superstability of micrometer viscous jets surrounded by weakly-elastic viscous shells
item.description: arXiv:2610.26150v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Our experiments demonstrate the strong stabilizing effect of a viscoelastic shell on flow-focused viscous jets. The results suggest that stabilization occurs when the polymer viscosity, $\eta_p$, exceeds a critical threshold, provided the extensional relaxation time, $\lambda$, is large enough to allow the polymer molecules to undergo the coil-stretch transition. Under these conditions, substantial extensional viscoelastic stresses develop as the liquid accelerates. Since both $\eta_p$ and $\lambda$ increase with shell viscosity, the polymer concentration required to stabilize the viscous jet decreases accordingly. Remarkably, moderately to highly viscous jets can be stabilized with very small polymer concentrations, for which no beads-on-a-string (BOAS) instability is observed.
item.dc:creator: A. Rubio-Gonz\'alez, D. Fern\'andez-Mart\'inez, M. Vakili, J. M. Montanero

item.title: Comprehensive Analysis of Relative Pressure Estimation in Type B Aortic Dissection Utilizing 4D-Flow MRI
item.description: arXiv:2503.02847v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can estimate three-dimensional (3D) time-resolved blood velocity fields using 4D-flow MRI, providing rich relative pressure field information. Clinical alternatives---catheterization and Doppler echocardiography---provide one-dimensional pressure drops. While the accuracy of one-dimensional pressure drops from 4D-flow has been explored, the accuracy of 3D relative pressure field estimates requires further evaluation. This work analyzes three state-of-the-art relative pressure estimators: virtual Work-Energy Relative Pressure (vWERP), the Pressure Poisson Estimator (PPE), and the Stokes Estimator (STE). Spatiotemporal characteristics and noise sensitivity were determined in silico via comparison with CFD-derived relative pressure fields. Estimators were then validated using a type B aortic dissection (TBAD) flow phantom with varying tear geometry and twelve catheter pressure measurements. Finally, each estimator was evaluated across eight patient cases in a clinical feasibility analysis. Estimators were cross-compared and evaluated for coherence since no reference catheter pressure measurements were available. PPE outperformed STE in the in silico relative pressure analysis, while both outperformed vWERP in plane-to-plane assessment. High velocity gradients and low spatial resolution contributed most significantly to local variations in 3D relative pressure field errors. Low temporal resolution led to systematic underestimation of highly transient peak pressure events. In the flow phantom analysis, vWERP was the most accurate method, followed by STE and then PPE. Each relative pressure estimator was strongly correlated with ground truth relative pressure values, despite the tendency to underestimate peak relative pressure. Patient case results demonstrated that each relative pressure estimator could be feasibly integrated into a clinical workflow.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Trans. Med. Imaging, 2026, early access
item.dc:creator: Brandon Hardy, Judith Zimmermann, Vincent Lechner, Mia Bonini, Julio A. Sotelo, Nicholas S. Burris, Daniel B. Ennis, David Marlevi, David A. Nordsletten

item.title: A mass invariant in a compressible turbulent medium
item.description: arXiv:2504.05469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting the measurable statistical properties of density fluctuations in a supersonic compressible turbulent flow is a major challenge in physics. In 1951, Chandrasekhar derived an invariant under the assumption of the statistical homogeneity and isotropy of the turbulent density field and stationarity of the background density. Recently, Jaupart & Chabrier (2021) extended this invariant to non-isotropic flows in a time-evolving background and showed that it has the dimension of a mass. This invariant $M_{\rm inv}$ is defined by $M_{\rm inv} = \mathbb{E}(\rho)\text{Var}\left(\frac{\rho}{\mathbb{E}(\rho)}\right)(l_{\rm c}^\rho)^3$ where $\rho$ is the density field and $l_{\rm c}^\rho$ is the correlation length. In this article, we perform numerical simulations of homogeneous and isotropic compressible turbulence to test the validity of this invariant in a medium subject to isotropic decaying turbulence. We study several input configurations, namely different Mach numbers, injection lengths of turbulence and equations of state. We confirm that $M_{\rm inv}$ remains constant during the decaying phase of turbulence. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical model of the density field statistics which predicts without any free parameter the evolution of the correlation length with the variance of the logdensity field beyond the assumption of the gaussian field for the logdensity. Noting that $M_{\rm inv}$ is independent of the Mach number, we show that this invariant can be used to relate the non-gaussian evolution of the logdensity probability distribution function to its variance with no free parameters.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Dumond, J\'er\'emy Fensch, Gilles Chabrier, Etienne Jaupart

item.title: IRENE: a fluId layeR finitE-elemeNt softwarE
item.description: arXiv:2506.17827v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a finite-element software library, IRENE, which allows to solve numerically the dynamics of a viscous fluid layer embedded in three-dimensional space. Unlike finite-element libraries present in the literature, IRENE can handle two-dimensional open surfaces with a wide range of boundary conditions, and inter-surface obstacles with any shapes, and is built upon the user-friendly and versatile finite element computational software (FEniCS). Also, the library can describe a wide range of physical regimes--both low-Reynolds-number and inertia-dominated ones--capturing the complex coupling between in-plane flows, out-of-plane deformations, surface tension, and elastic response. We validate IRENE against known analytical and numerical results, and demonstrate its capabilities through physical examples. Overall, IRENE provides a versatile and efficient tool for understanding fluid-layer dynamics on multiple physical scales, from flows of lipidic membranes on a microscopic level, to fluid flows on a macroscopic scale, to atmospheric air flows on a planetary level.
item.dc:creator: Dennis W\"orthm\"uller, Gaetano Ferraro, Pierre Sens, Michele Castellana

item.title: Physics-informed data-driven inference of an interpretable equivariant LES model of two-dimensional incompressible fluid turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2602.15743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Restrictive phenomenological assumptions limit the accuracy and generality of subgrid-scale models of fluid turbulence, especially in flows where coherent structures and bidirectional energy transfer play an important dynamical role. This paper introduces a symbolic, physically-informed data-driven subgrid-scale closure for two-dimensional incompressible turbulence. The closure is inferred from filtered direct numerical simulation data using symmetry-constrained sparse regression, together with dimensional-consistency constraints on the inferred coefficients. While the model is inferred using LES-style spatial coarse-graining, its structure is found to be more similar to RANS models, as it employs an additional field to describe the dynamics of unresolved scales. For the range of two-dimensional benchmark flows considered here, the inferred model substantially improves upon widely used LES models, yielding accurate predictions of subgrid-scale stresses, local and global fluxes between different scales, and other key quantities in both a priori and a posteriori benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Ugliotti, Brandon Choi, Mateo Reynoso, Daniel R. Gurevich, Roman O. Grigoriev

item.title: A neural operator framework for data-driven discovery of stability and receptivity in physical systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.19465v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how complex systems respond to perturbations, such as whether they will remain stable or what their most sensitive patterns are, is a fundamental challenge across science and engineering. Traditional stability and receptivity (resolvent) analyses are powerful but rely on known equations and linearization, limiting their use in nonlinear or poorly modeled systems. Here, we introduce a data-driven framework that automatically identifies stability properties and optimal forcing responses from observation data alone, without requiring governing equations. By training a neural network as a dynamics emulator and using automatic differentiation to extract its Jacobian, we can compute eigenmodes and resolvent modes directly from data. We demonstrate the method on both canonical chaotic models and high-dimensional fluid flows, successfully identifying dominant instability modes and input-output structures even in strongly nonlinear regimes. By leveraging a neural network-based emulator, we readily obtain a nonlinear representation of system dynamics while additionally retrieving intricate dynamical patterns that were previously difficult to resolve. This equation-free methodology establishes a broadly applicable tool for analyzing complex, high-dimensional datasets, with immediate relevance to grand challenges in fields such as climate science, neuroscience, and fluid engineering.
item.dc:creator: Chengyun Wang, Liwei Chen, Nils Thuerey

item.title: Squid funnels time their elastic recoil to amplify pulsed jets
item.description: arXiv:2605.03239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pulsed jets propel squid across nearly four orders of magnitude in body size. Each pulse leaves through the funnel, a soft nozzle, but whether its compliance acts within a pulse is not known. We tracked chromatophores on two squid species and found that the funnel dilates and recoils, with a repeatable phase lag, while the mantle is still contracting, and that the lag persists after denervation. For inertia-dominated jets, silicone nozzles, 3D fluid-structure simulations and a reduced-order model agree that the impulse reaches about 4$\times$ the rigid value when the nozzle response time is 0.2 to 0.4 of the jet-acceleration time, a range that overlaps the in vivo timing. The wall stores strain energy during acceleration and returns it during expulsion (akin to an elastic capacitor), which we term "superpropulsion". Synthetic nozzles tuned for superpropulsion launch jets farther in air, disperse dye faster, and drive a boat faster at a lower cost of transport.
item.dc:creator: Daehyun Choi, Paras Singh, Ian Bergerson, Minho Kim, Jieun Park, Halley J. Wallace, Kenny Zhang, Sandy Y. Hsieh, Aqua T. Asberry, Theodore A. Uyeno, William F. Gilly, Hyungmin Park, Daeshik Kang, Chandan Bose, Saad Bhamla

item.title: Coarse-grained local available potential energy
item.description: arXiv:2605.15879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The available potential energy (APE) of a fluid can be defined locally in space, providing useful insights into both the energetics and dynamics of stratified flows ranging from three-dimensional turbulence to planetary scale circulations. Here we develop a framework for considering the multi-scale evolution of the local APE using a spatial filtering, or coarse-graining, approach. A scale decomposition valid generally for filters with both horizontal and vertical support is proposed, and shown to admit a construction in terms of a series of band-passed energies. The physical interpretation of the decomposition is discussed, and evolution equations for the APE at scales larger, and smaller, than the filtering scale are derived --- including the cross-scale APE flux term. These results can be paired with existing frameworks for coarse-grained kinetic energy, offering the potential for examining a complete energy cycle that accounts for conversions between both spatial scales and energy reservoirs. An illustrative example of the application of this approach to a simulation of three-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is provided, including an exact formulation of the scale-dependent instability energy budgets, and the distribution of terms such as cross-scale transfers and APE dissipation in physical space.
item.dc:creator: Jacob O. Wenegrat, Tomas Chor, Roy Barkan

item.title: A real-variable unidirectional reduction of deep-water gravity waves
item.description: arXiv:2605.24997v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A unidirectional reduction of the deep-water surface gravity wave problem is derived in physical space using real variables. By employing a near-identity canonical transformation, cubic interactions are eliminated from the Hamiltonian, resulting in a bidirectional system analogous to the 1D Zakharov equation. An exact factorization of the linear dynamics then selects the rightward-propagating branch, which is carried to second order in the wave steepness, yielding a single nonlocal evolution equation with full linear dispersion. The model admits an exact monochromatic solution whose reconstructed surface elevation is the third-order Stokes wave, and a multiple-scales analysis recovers the Dysthe envelope equation complete with its nonlocal mean-flow term. The equation also admits exact breather solutions, whose profiles agree closely with those of the super compact equation. Dropping the sub-leading nonlinear terms that vanish on the resonant manifold provides a more compact variant suitable for analytical study. Numerical comparisons show that both formulations track the fully nonlinear Euler dynamics closely through modulational-instability recurrence and broadband focusing up to moderate wave steepness.
item.dc:creator: P\"aivo Simson

item.title: Particle settling in turbidity currents: concentration-gradient-driven biased sampling
item.description: arXiv:2606.08241v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the mechanisms governing particle settling in turbidity currents using Eulerian$\unicode{x2013}$Lagrangian direct numerical simulations. The Eulerian carrier flow is driven either by solutal buoyancy or particle feedback, with the Lagrangian phase comprising passive tracers or inertial particles, respectively. The effective particle settling velocity is decomposed into a fluid velocity sampled at particle positions and a particle-fluid slip velocity. The Eulerian mean profiles of these velocities are obtained using a concentration-weighted average of the coarse-grained fields. The mean sampled fluid velocity is shown to be approximately equal to the ratio of the vertical turbulent flux of particles to their mean concentration and reflects biased sampling of upward turbulent fluctuations at particle positions, despite the zero Eulerian mean vertical fluid velocity. The passive-tracer cases show that the upward bias does not require particle inertia and arises from turbulent transport acting on concentration gradients, as it persists for inhomogeneous tracer seeding but disappears under uniform seeding. For the weakly inertial regime considered here, the upward bias dominates downward-directed biases associated with particle inertia. The mean slip velocity is well approximated by the terminal settling velocity predicted for a quiescent fluid. This is consistent with a leading-order balance between buoyancy and drag in the slope-normal direction. Modelling the sampled fluid velocity from the turbulent flux and using the slip-velocity approximation yield an Eulerian prediction for the settling velocity, in good agreement with the simulation data for the dilute, weakly inertial particles considered.
item.dc:creator: Lianzheng Cui, Eric Climent, Graham O. Hughes, Maarten van Reeuwijk

item.title: Translation dynamics of evaporating sessile binary-mixture droplet populations
item.description: arXiv:2606.11388v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The translation dynamics of two binary mixture droplets is investigated theoretically and is corroborated with experiments. The proposed model accounts for the effects of Marangoni stresses generated by evaporative cooling and concentration gradients, as well as vapour diffusion, for both components of the binary mixture. We consider thin droplets, allowing us to use the lubrication theory to derive the evolution equation for the droplet profiles. We numerically solve the evolution equations using the finite element method and examine various cases of pure and binary droplet pairs exhibiting translational behaviours like attraction, repulsion, and 'chasing'. The results show that the combined effect of solutal Marangoni, capillary effect, and thermal Marangoni determines the movement of the droplets. The non-uniform evaporation generated from 'vapour shielding' creates such effects. We observe that for droplets with the same initial composition, solutal Marangoni and capillary forces induce droplet attraction, while thermal Marangoni effects drive their repulsion. For droplets with different initial compositions, the drop with a higher concentration of the more volatile component pushes, or `chases', the drop with a lower initial concentration of this component, completely driven by the solutal Marangoni. We carried out experiments involving water-morpholine binary mixture droplets to validate the results predicted by our model.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Debnath, Anna Malachtari, George Karapetsas, Daniel Orejon, Khellil Sefiane, Alidad Amirfazli, Omar K. Matar, Prashant Valluri

item.title: Bi-stable Nonlinear Energy Sinks (BNESs) for Response Mitigation and Drag Reduction of Subsea Cables Undergoing Vortex-induced Vibrations
item.description: arXiv:2606.22638v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A methodology for passive mitigation of vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) in subsea dynamic power cables is developed using optimized, strongly nonlinear bi-stable mass-spring-damper attachments, termed bi-stable nonlinear energy sinks (BNESs), within the open-source MoorDyn library. A fully three-dimensional time-domain framework captures cable dynamics, Morison-type hydrodynamic forcing, nonlinear vibration-mitigation mechanisms, and spatially and temporally varying currents. The BNESs are consistently integrated into the cable model, allowing treatment of highly non-stationary VIVs. A data-driven optimization study samples the BNES design space across multiple current profiles and shows that properly tuned configurations substantially reduce peak-to-peak cable vibration amplitudes. The BNESs also produce significant and robust reductions in cumulative VIV-induced energy intake from the surrounding flow and in drag energy. To the authors' knowledge, passive nonlinear attachments are shown for the first time to reduce both energy intake and drag amplification in a subsea cable, with potential benefits for short- and long-term fatigue. Time-frequency wavelet analysis reveals targeted nonlinear energy transfers and scattering from dominant high-amplitude, low-frequency cable modes to lower-amplitude, higher-frequency modes. This modal redistribution promotes rapid dissipation through hydrodynamic damping and internal structural losses, explaining the simultaneous reductions in vibration amplitude and cumulative energy intake. The results demonstrate that BNESs can provide effective and robust VIV mitigation for subsea power cables under realistic unsteady operating conditions and motivate future studies involving combined current-wave loading, platform-induced motion, and fatigue-life assessment.
item.dc:creator: Anargyros Michaloliakos, Ryan Davies, Matthew Hall, Alexander F. Vakakis

item.title: Flow in a porous non-axisymmetric annular conduit: Coupling wall compliance and peristalsis
item.description: arXiv:2607.15239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coenen \textit{et al.}\ (\textit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol.~921, 2021, p.~R2) developed a reduced-order model of peristaltic pumping in non-axisymmetric annular conduits with rigid walls, in the context of periarterial space (PAS) flows. \textit{In vivo} studies show that the PAS's outer wall undergoes significant displacement due to flow within and that the penetrating PASs form a porous pathway. To account for these biomechanical aspects, we revisit the problem of flow in an eccentric annular conduit and incorporate porous drag and two-way-coupled fluid--structure interaction between the compliant outer wall and the cerebrospinal fluid flow within. A Darcy--Brinkman term in the axial momentum equation accounts for drag due to the porous medium. We account for changes in hydraulic resistance due to peristalsis and compliant-wall displacements perturbatively, thereby reducing the problem to a single nonlinear partial differential equation for the axial pressure. This reduced-order model allows us to build a mechanistic understanding of flow through a porous penetrating PAS and enables parametric studies. For small-amplitude peristaltic waves, analytical solutions are possible.
item.dc:creator: Nishanth Surianarayanan, Ivan C. Christov

item.title: Lattice Boltzmann Methods for Navier-Stokes Equations in General Orthogonal Coordinates for Efficient Flow Simulations using Nonuniform Clustered Grids
item.description: arXiv:2607.15362v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resolving multiscale fluid flows or boundary layers effectively requires the use of nonuniform meshes with local grid clustering. The standard lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), a kinetic theory-based approach for computational fluid dynamics, however, is restricted to the use of uniform Cartesian grids. We present new and improved formulations of the LBM that accommodate continuously varying spatial grids via coordinate transformations to simulate the Navier-Stokes equations (NSE) in the general orthogonal coordinates (GOC). They are constructed using a Chapman-Enskog analysis to specify the equilibrium moments of the distribution functions and the geometric force terms used in the collision step to be dependent on the local metric factors and their spatial derivatives, along with the density, momentum and their fluxes, and some correction terms related to the normal velocity gradients so as to accurately represent the NSE in the GOC. The resulting GOC-LBM importantly maintains the simplicity of the collide-and-stream approach and is Galilean invariant that is free of the cubic velocity artifacts. Our GOC-LBM is general and modular in that it can be used with any collision model with appropriate modifications to the equilibria and forcing terms. We present its implementation details for a variety of collision models while the central moments-based model using multiple relaxation times was found to be the most robust in practical implementations. We validate the GOC-LBM through numerical simulations for various benchmark flow problems. Moreover, we demonstrate significant computational advantages of our approach for a case study on simulating boundary layer flows efficiently that involves coupling the GOC-LBM for the NSE with a new GOC-LB scheme for solving the magnetic induction equation for magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), and for another case study involving orthogonal curvilinear grids.
item.dc:creator: Eman Yahia, Kannan Premnath, William Schupbach

item.title: Neptuna: A Comprehensive Machine Learning Framework for Benchmarking Complex Multiphase Flows
item.description: arXiv:2607.22280v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Compressible multiphase flows involving shocks and material interfaces arise in applications such as bubble collapse and droplet breakup, where strong nonlinear interactions produce complex interface deformation, mixing, and multiscale dynamics. Developing reliable machine learning surrogates for these flows remains challenging due to the simultaneous presence of compressibility, sharp discontinuities, and multiphase effects. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed for shock-driven compressible multiphase flows, comprising 3 TB of high-fidelity 2D and 3D datasets featuring shock-induced bubble collapse and droplet breakup. We evaluate diverse surrogate model families on our benchmarking framework: Neptuna, including convolutional, spectral, transformer-based, and pre-trained PDE foundation models. Beyond standard MSE training, we investigate composite losses that combine MSE with Sobolev, interface-aware, and structure-aware terms, along with adaptive loss balancing using SoftAdapt and GradNorm. Evaluation includes pointwise, spectral, feature-focused, structural, and physics-informed metrics. Results show that no single model performs best across all datasets and metrics, while composite losses significantly improve interface preservation and spectral fidelity. Among adaptive weighting strategies, SoftAdapt provides the most consistent improvements with almost no overhead compared to MSE-only training. The benchmarking repository and the dataset are made available at \url{https://tumaer.github.io/Neptuna/}
item.dc:creator: Harish Ramachandran, Bj\"orn Kimpel, Thomas Paula, Josef Winter, Steffen Schmidt, Nikolaus Adams

item.title: Transparent 3D-printed flow cells for porous media studies with proof-of-concept on two-phase flow-reversal asymmetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.04105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Porous media experiments commonly rely on geometry-controlled and optically transparent experimental flow cells. Examples include studies of flow structure, solute mixing, multiphase flow, bacterial dynamics, and reactive transport. Here, we provide a reproducible and open-source protocol to fabricate transparent monolithic porous flow cells by stereolithography 3D printing. The protocol covers digital design, resin printing, internal flushing, and resin coating. The flushing and coating steps are central to the workflow, enabling enclosed single-material cells to be cleared of uncured resin and made optically transparent for direct imaging. The protocol produces optically transparent, millimetre-scale, and quasi-two-dimensional flow cells suitable for simultaneous pressure and image-based measurements. As a proof of concept, we study flow-reversal asymmetry in steady oil-air two-phase flow in quasi-two-dimensional Hele-Shaw cells containing either triangular or cylindrical obstacles. Directional differences are quantified from pressure measurements and from image-based active-width measurements. The triangular geometry produces a clear directional response, whereas the cylindrical geometry remains symmetric within experimental uncertainty. These results demonstrate that our fabrication protocol can link digitally designed pore geometries to macroscopic pressure response and steady-state two-phase flow organisation. By making the design files, scripts, and manufacturing workflow openly available, we aim to make 3D-printed flow cells readily adaptable to other experimental systems and research fields.
item.dc:creator: Yann Dumay, J. Kevin Pierce, Julie Delhaie, Pooja Singh, Erika Eiser

item.title: Equations of motion for dust particles in dust-collecting devices (Translated article from USSR Journal Otoplenie i Ventilyatsiya, No. 4 (1934): 27-29)
item.description: arXiv:2610.07315v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Preface for the English Translation: While checking out early USSR journal articles for our literature search, we recently had tremendous difficulty acquiring this 1934 Klyachko original publication through our library systems. After obtaining and reading a scanned copy of it supplied by the Russian library in Moscow, we realized that relatively scarce citations of this work in the Western literature are often accompanied by inaccurate descriptions and comments, indicating that most Western authors might have gotten only second-hand knowledge about it and never seemed to have read the original article. Compared with various correlation formulas in the modern literature, the Klyachko 1934 formula for sphere drag in fluid flow appears to be the most elegant and cleanest one thus far. Therefore, we decided to make an effort to translate this historical work and publish it in the open literature to facilitate its accessibility to English readers worldwide.
item.dc:creator: L. S. Klyachko (Translators: Carlos A A. Ram{\i}rez, James Q. Feng,,Rodney J. Kubesh)

item.title: Structure of Turbulent Radiative Mixing Layers
item.description: arXiv:2509.03802v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Turbulent radiative mixing layers (TRMLs), where shear-driven turbulence mixes dense and diffuse gas into rapidly cooling intermediate-temperature gas, are ubiquitous in the interstellar and circumgalactic media. A Reynolds decomposition of 3D simulations shows that a cooling-driven compressive stress creates a pressure dip that sustains a steady inflow of hot gas, and that radiative losses are balanced mainly by enthalpy advection, not turbulent heat flux. Contrary to previous claims, the cooling rate per unit area saturates and becomes independent of box size in the strong-cooling limit.
item.dc:creator: Prateek Sharma, Arnav Kumar, Dipayan Datta, Arif Babul, Rishita Das, Konduri Aditya

item.title: Computing statistical solutions of a Mach 2000 astrophysical jet
item.description: arXiv:2605.25282v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The multi-dimensional compressible Euler equations admit non-unique entropy solutions in turbulent regimes, and extreme-Mach astrophysical flows are a natural setting in which this breakdown of deterministic well-posedness becomes computationally visible. We compute statistical solutions of a Mach~2000 astrophysical jet, defined as the pushforward of an initial probability measure through a vectorial lattice Boltzmann method, by Monte Carlo sampling with $M=1000$ realizations on grids of up to $12.8$ million cells. Under mesh refinement the individual realizations diverge pathwise, while the statistical solution converges: Wasserstein distances of the one- and two-point marginals, the ensemble mean, and the ensemble standard deviation all exhibit stable positive convergence rates. A spatially resolved analysis along the jet axis traces this dichotomy to the structure of the one-point laws, which are numerically Dirac in the undisturbed core, skewed in the sheared turbulent regions, and intermittent two-state mixtures at the random leading front. We conclude that the computed statistical solution is non-Dirac and remains stable in the extreme compressible regime, in which no strong solution is expected to exist.
item.dc:creator: Stephan Simonis, Gauthier Wissocq

item.title: Evaporation-Driven Nanowire Self-Assembly in an Elongated Droplet
item.description: arXiv:2607.06794v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Drying of nanowire-laden elongated droplets is a ubiquitous process in printed electronics fabrication, where the resulting deposition pattern critically determines device performance by controlling nanowire alignment, connectivity, and percolating charge-transport pathways. However, the physical understanding of evaporation-driven deposition is still largely derived from studies of spherical droplets on homogeneous substrates. This gap limits the ability to predict and control deposit morphology in realistic printing scenarios. Here, we use mesoscale lattice Boltzmann simulations to investigate the drying of nanowire-laden elongated droplets on wettability-patterned substrates, focusing on the effects of droplet geometry, nanowire interactions, and nanowire length. The elongated droplet geometry is found to intrinsically induce distinct axial and transverse inhomogeneities in the final deposit. Increasing the effective attraction between nanowires, which mimics changes in surface chemistry or solvent conditions, can improve electrical connectivity but also promotes clustering and local ordering, reducing structural uniformity. In contrast, increasing nanowire length yields a dual benefit by improving long-range connectivity while simultaneously enhancing deposit homogeneity. Our findings provide design guidance for balancing electrical transport and structural uniformity in evaporation-driven printed electronics.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Sch\"ottner, Qingguang Xie, Jens Harting

item.title: Accretion Rates and Thermohaline Convection in Polluted White Dwarfs
item.description: arXiv:2608.31110v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Polluted white dwarfs provide a unique window into the composition of exoplanetary material, but interpreting their surface abundances requires a quantitative understanding of the mixing processes in their envelopes. Accretion of metal-rich debris onto hydrogen-rich white dwarfs drives thermohaline (fingering) convection in the underlying radiative zone. Previous studies have modeled this as enhanced diffusive transport, often inferring mass accretion rates, $\dot{M}_{\rm acc}$, that exceed constraints from X-ray observations. Here we develop a time-dependent model that treats thermohaline mixing as a propagating front whose evolution is coupled self-consistently to the surface abundance of heavy elements. We perform hydrodynamical simulations which demonstrate that thermohaline mixing drives the composition gradient towards marginal stability. Using this condition, we derive analytic solutions in shallow and deep stratification regimes, finding that the mixed layer depth, $h$, and surface abundance, $X_{\rm surf}$, both scale as $t^{1/2}$ at early times, transitioning to $h \propto t^{4/27}$ and $X_{\rm surf} \propto t^{10/27}$ at later times. The mixed layer reaches depths of only $\sim 100$ km over $10^5$ yr and, without gravitational settling, never reaches a steady state. Including settling leads to an equilibrium surface abundance scaling as $X_{\rm surf, eq} \propto \dot{M}_{\rm acc}^{30/43}$. Applied to G 29--38, the model matches the observed heavy-element abundance for $\dot{M}_{\rm acc} \sim 2\times 10^9$--$4\times 10^{9}~\mathrm{g~s^{-1}}$, in better agreement with X-ray constraints than prior estimates incorporating thermohaline mixing. We also present a general scaling relation for inferring accretion rates directly from observed surface abundances and stellar properties, giving a practical prescription for other polluted white dwarfs.
item.dc:creator: J. R. Fuentes, Matias Castro-Tapia, Jim Fuller, Marcus King
